title: Lost Joseph will come back
intro: This is one of the best-loved ghazals of Hafez (about 1315–1390), and perhaps the most consoling poem in Persian: every couplet ends with the same two words, *gham makhor*, 'do not grieve'. It begins with the story of Joseph (Yusof), which Iranians know from the Quran and from poetry. His jealous brothers threw him into a well and told their father Jacob that a wolf had eaten him; Jacob wept in his 'house of sorrows' in Canaan until he went blind, and years later Joseph's shirt, sent from Egypt, gave him back his sight. Hafez turns that story into a promise: what is lost comes back, the wheel of time turns, and no road is without an end.

lines.fa: یوسف گم‌گشته باز آید به کنعان غم مخور / کلبه‌ی احزان شود روزی گلستان غم مخور
lines.r: yusof-e gom-gashte bāz āyad be kan'ān gham makhor / kolbe-ye ahzān shavad ruzi golestān gham makhor
lines.en: Lost Joseph will come back to Canaan – do not grieve; / the house of sorrows will one day be a rose garden – do not grieve.
words: Joseph, the most beautiful of men
lines.faV: یوسُفِ گُم‌گَشته باز آیَد به کَنعان غَم مَخور / کُلبه‌یِ اَحزان شَوَد روزی گُلِستان غَم مَخور

lines.fa: ای دل غمدیده حالت به شود دل بد مکن / وین سر شوریده باز آید به سامان غم مخور
lines.r: ey del-e ghamdide hāl-at beh shavad del bad makon / vin sar-e shuride bāz āyad be sāmān gham makhor
lines.en: O grieving heart, you will feel better – do not lose heart; / this troubled head will come back to its senses – do not grieve.
lines.faV: اَی دِلِ غَمدیده حالَت بِه شَوَد دِل بَد مَکُن / وین سَرِ شوریده باز آیَد به سامان غَم مَخور

lines.fa: گر بهار عمر باشد باز بر تخت چمن / چتر گل در سر کشی ای مرغ خوشخوان غم مخور
lines.r: gar bahār-e 'omr bāshad bāz bar takht-e chaman / chatr-e gol dar sar keshi ey morgh-e khoshkhān gham makhor
lines.en: If life brings spring again, on the throne of the meadow / you will hold a parasol of roses over your head, sweet singer – do not grieve.
lines.faV: گَر بَهارِ عُمر باشَد باز بَر تَختِ چَمَن / چَترِ گُل دَر سَر کِشی اَی مُرغِ خوشخوان غَم مَخور

lines.fa: دور گردون گر دو روزی بر مراد ما نرفت / دائماً یکسان نباشد حال دوران غم مخور
lines.r: dowr-e gardun gar do ruzi bar morād-e mā naraft / dā'eman yeksān nabāshad hāl-e dowrān gham makhor
lines.en: If the turning sky has gone against us for a day or two, / the times are not always the same – do not grieve.
words: a day or two, a short while
lines.faV: دَورِ گَردون گَر دو روزی بَر مُرادِ ما نَرَفت / دائِماً یِکسان نَباشَد حالِ دَوران غَم مَخور

lines.fa: هان مشو نومید چون واقف نه‌ای از سر غیب / باشد اندر پرده بازی‌های پنهان غم مخور
lines.r: hān masho nowmid chon vāghef na-'i az serr-e gheyb / bāshad andar parde bāzi-hā-ye penhān gham makhor
lines.en: Take care, do not despair: you do not know the secret of the unseen; / there may be hidden games behind the curtain – do not grieve.
lines.note: «پشت پرده» 'behind the curtain' is still the everyday Persian for what goes on out of sight.
words: take care!, look! – an old interjection
lines.faV: هان مَشو نَومید چون واقِف نه‌ای اَز سِرِّ غَیب / باشَد اَندَر پَرده بازی‌هایِ پِنهان غَم مَخور

lines.fa: ای دل ار سیل فنا بنیاد هستی برکند / چون تو را نوح است کشتیبان ز طوفان غم مخور
lines.r: ey del ar seyl-e fanā bonyād-e hasti bar-kanad / chon to rā nuh ast kashtibān ze tufān gham makhor
lines.en: O heart, if the flood of death tears up the foundations of being, / with Noah as your boatman, do not grieve over the Flood.
lines.note: طوفان here is the Flood of Noah; today it means any storm.
lines.faV: اَی دِل اَر سَیلِ فَنا بُنیادِ هَستی بَرکَنَد / چون تو را نوح اَست کَشتیبان ز طوفان غَم مَخور

lines.fa: در بیابان گر به شوق کعبه خواهی زد قدم / سرزنش‌ها گر کند خار مغیلان غم مخور
lines.r: dar biyābān gar be showgh-e ka'be khāhi zad ghadam / sarzanesh-hā gar konad khār-e moghilān gham makhor
lines.en: If you set out across the desert, longing for the Kaaba, / and the acacia thorns reproach you – do not grieve.
lines.note: Pilgrims who crossed the Arabian desert were torn by acacia thorns; in poetry the thorns are the hardships, and the critics, on the way to any goal.
words: the thorns of the desert acacia
lines.faV: دَر بیابان گَر به شَوقِ کَعبه خواهی زَد قَدَم / سَرزَنِش‌ها گَر کُنَد خارِ مُغیلان غَم مَخور

lines.fa: گرچه منزل بس خطرناک است و مقصد بس بعید / هیچ راهی نیست کان را نیست پایان غم مخور
lines.r: garche manzel bas khatarnāk ast o maghsad bas ba'id / hich rāhi nist kān rā nist pāyān gham makhor
lines.en: Though the stages are very dangerous and the goal very far, / there is no road that has no end – do not grieve.
words: stage of a journey, stopping place
lines.faV: گَرچه مَنزِل بَس خَطَرناک اَست و مَقصَد بَس بَعید / هیچ راهی نیست کان را نیست پایان غَم مَخور

lines.fa: حال ما در فرقت جانان و ابرام رقیب / جمله می‌داند خدای حال‌گردان غم مخور
lines.r: hāl-e mā dar forghat-e jānān o ebrām-e raghib / jomle mi-dānad khodā-ye hāl-gardān gham makhor
lines.en: How we fare, far from the beloved and pestered by the rival – / God, who changes every state, knows it all; do not grieve.
lines.note: The prayer Iranians say at the moment the New Year begins calls God «محول الحول و الاحوال», 'the one who changes the years and the states' – the same God as Hafez's خدای حال‌گردان.
words: the rival in love, the watchful guard
God – the older form of خدا
lines.faV: حالِ ما دَر فُرقَتِ جانان و اِبرامِ رَقیب / جُمله می‌دانَد خُدایِ حال‌گَردان غَم مَخور

lines.fa: حافظا در کنج فقر و خلوت شب‌های تار / تا بود وردت دعا و درس قرآن غم مخور
lines.r: hāfezā dar konj-e faghr o khalvat-e shab-hā-ye tār / tā bovad verd-at do'ā vo dars-e ghor'ān gham makhor
lines.en: Hafez, in your corner of poverty and in the solitude of dark nights, / as long as prayer and the Quran are your daily practice, do not grieve.
lines.note: Hafez's pen name means 'one who knows the Quran by heart', which he did.
words: a prayer said every day, a daily practice
lines.faV: حافِظا دَر کُنجِ فَقر و خَلوَتِ شَب‌هایِ تار / تا بُوَد وِردَت دُعا و دَرسِ قُرآن غَم مَخور

commentary:
**The images.** Hafez gathers every picture of hope he can find. First the stories everyone knows: Joseph coming home to Canaan, Jacob's hut of sorrows turning into a rose garden, Noah steering his ark through the Flood. Then nature: a songbird that will sit enthroned in the meadow, under a parasol of roses, when spring comes back. Then the journey: a pilgrim crossing the desert to Mecca, torn by thorns, on a road that may be long and dangerous but must have an end. And above all the turning sky, [[دور گردون|dowr-e gardun]], which never stays still – what has gone against us will come round again.

**The rhythm.** The ghazal is in *ramal*, a long, rolling metre: *DUM-da-DUM-DUM DUM-da-DUM-DUM DUM-da-DUM-DUM DUM-da-DUM*. Listen to *yu-so-fe gom-gash-te bā-zā-yad be kan-'ān gham ma-khor*. Every couplet ends in the same rhyme – [[کنعان|kan'ān]], [[گلستان|golestān]], [[سامان|sāmān]], [[خوشخوان|khoshkhān]], [[دوران|dowrān]] – followed by the same refrain, [[غم مخور|gham makhor]]: a [[ردیف|radif]] so strong that the whole poem feels like one long, patient reassurance.

**The grammar.** The language is close to today's. The old negative imperative uses [[م|ma-]]: [[مخور|makhor]] 'don't eat', [[مشو|masho]] 'don't become', [[مکن|makon]] 'don't do'. [[گر|gar]] and [[ار|ar]] are short for [[اگر|agar]]; [[نه‌ای|na-'i]] is [[نیستی|nisti]] 'you are not'; [[نومید|nowmid]] is [[ناامید|nā-omid]]. And [[غم خوردن|gham khordan]], 'to eat sorrow', is still the everyday word for 'to worry'. Couplet 4 in modern prose: [[اگر چرخ روزگار دو روزی به میل ما نچرخید، غصه نخور؛ اوضاع دنیا همیشه یکسان نمی‌ماند|agar charkh-e ruzgār do ruzi be meyl-e mā nacharkhid, ghosse nakhor; owzā'-e donyā hamishe yeksān nemi-mānad]].

**Using it.** This is the ghazal Iranians send to a friend in trouble, and many people know its first line by heart. [[یوسف گم‌گشته باز آید به کنعان|yusof-e gom-gashte bāz āyad be kan'ān]] is said when someone long absent comes home, and [[هیچ راهی نیست کان را نیست پایان|hich rāhi nist kān rā nist pāyān]] to anyone who thinks a hard time will never end.
